genesis-1-26-27.title: Genesis 1:26-27
genesis-1-26-27.summary: Let us make man in our image, and then a singular verb does the making.
genesis-1-26-27.plain: The real question: why does God say “let us make” and then act alone in the very next line? The candidates are multiple gods, the Trinity, or something else. **Let's build a shed. I built a shed.** The first sentence includes other people. The second one says who actually swung the hammer. Both can be true about the same shed, and nobody thinks the second sentence contradicts the first. This card reads it as an announcement to a real council, not a description of who did the work.
genesis-1-26-27.prob: God speaks in the plural and then acts in the singular, one verse apart. Any reading has to account for both halves, and most accounts only handle one.
genesis-1-26-27.res: Read as an announcement to the council rather than a description of who does the work, both halves stand. Verse 26 addresses a room. Verse 27 records a single actor.

psalm-82.title: Psalm 82
psalm-82.summary: God stands in the divine assembly and passes sentence on the elohim He put in charge.
psalm-82.plain: The real question: are “the gods” here actual spiritual beings under God's authority, or just a poetic name for human judges? **Animal** covers a whale and a mouse. It tells you what kind of thing something is, not how big or how important. Now imagine your only word for human also worked that way, so a king and a newborn got the same label, and rank had to come from somewhere else in the sentence. This card reads “the gods” as real, corrupt spiritual beings under God, not human judges.
psalm-82.prob: Four moves in eight verses, and one reading has to carry all four. Verse 1 has God standing in an assembly of elohim. Verse 6 calls them sons of the Most High. Verse 7 sentences them to die like men. Verse 8 asks God to arise and inherit all the nations.
psalm-82.res: Divine beings holding delegated authority over the nations, judged for misrule, accounts for every one. Verse 6 names what they are, verse 7 strips it, and verse 8 asks for the allotment itself to be revoked. That closing line is why this psalm is the hinge rather than one passage among many: it is a prayer that the arrangement in Deuteronomy 32:8-9 come to an end. The two passages are one argument read from opposite ends.

1-kings-22-19-23.title: 1 Kings 22:19-23
1-kings-22-19-23.summary: Micaiah reports seeing Yahweh enthroned with the host standing to His right and left.
1-kings-22-19-23.plain: The real question: is this an actual exchange between God and other beings, or just a dramatic way of narrating a decision God already made alone? **Picture a commander asking a room for volunteers, someone stepping forward with a plan, and the commander approving it before sending them out.** That's a conversation with genuine give and take, not one person narrating a decision to themselves. This card takes it as exactly that: a real council with deliberation to match.
1-kings-22-19-23.prob: A prophet describes God asking for volunteers and approving a plan He could have executed alone. The scene is hard to read as figurative when the plan is then carried out.
1-kings-22-19-23.res: A council with actual members, genuine deliberation, and delegated execution accounts for the question, the volunteer, and the outcome without treating the vision as decorative.

job-1-6-12.title: Job 1:6-12
job-1-6-12.summary: The sons of God present themselves and the satan comes among them.
job-1-6-12.plain: The real question: is “the satan” here the devil's proper name, or a job title for a prosecuting role in God's court? **"The accountant" names a job. "Mr. Accountant" would sound odd,** because accountant is doing the work of a title there, not a name. A figure in an old story gets introduced with "the" in front of a role-word the same way. That marks an office, not a specific someone. He's holding a position, not wearing a name badge. This card reads “the satan” as an office, not a name.
job-1-6-12.prob: There is a scheduled convening, an attendance report, and a figure who must ask permission before acting. None of that fits a freelance enemy of God.
job-1-6-12.res: An office within an assembly explains the attendance, the permission, and the limits placed on him in the same stroke.

psalm-89-5-7.title: Psalm 89:5-7
psalm-89-5-7.summary: Yahweh is feared in the council of the holy ones, and nothing in the skies compares to Him.
psalm-89-5-7.plain: The real question: does “nothing compares to you” only work if there's something real in the room to compare against? **“Best goalkeeper in the world” only means something if other goalkeepers exist. Call yourself unmatched in an empty room and the word does no work.** The praise here runs on that same logic: actual rivals in the room, all of them outclassed. This card takes the “holy ones” as a real company of divine beings, not poetic flourish.
psalm-89-5-7.prob: The psalm proves God's uniqueness by comparing Him to others. A comparison to nothing proves nothing.
psalm-89-5-7.res: The company of divine beings makes the argument work as written. Incomparability among peers is a stronger claim than solitude.

isaiah-6-1-8.title: Isaiah 6:1-8
isaiah-6-1-8.summary: The throne room, the seraphim, and the plural question, who will go for us.
isaiah-6-1-8.plain: The real question: is this writer overhearing an actual conversation already in progress, or is “us” just a royal way of saying “me”? **Walk into a meeting already running and someone asks the room, “Who's going to take this one?” You don't have to ask who else is there. The question itself tells you the room isn't empty.** This vision reads the same way: a real council, mid-session, that Isaiah has just stepped into.
isaiah-6-1-8.prob: Who is the us. The question is addressed to someone, and Isaiah answers as though he has stepped into a conversation already running.
isaiah-6-1-8.res: A session in progress explains the plural, the cleansing before he may speak, and the fact that he volunteers rather than being commanded.

daniel-7-9-14.title: Daniel 7:9-14
daniel-7-9-14.summary: Thrones are set in place, plural, the court sits, and one like a son of man comes on the clouds.
daniel-7-9-14.plain: The real question: who fills the other thrones, and does a second enthroned figure split God into two? **A courtroom has a judge's bench and a jury box. Seeing “thrones were set in place” (plural) with only one figure named is like walking in and finding the jury box built before anyone tells you who's sitting there.** The seats being there is the point, even before the names are given. This card reads the extra thrones as filled and the second enthroned figure as a real co-ruler, not a rival god.
daniel-7-9-14.prob: Thrones is plural and the text never says who fills the others. A second figure then receives dominion that belongs to God alone.
daniel-7-9-14.res: A seated court with a second enthroned figure accounts for the plural, the books, and the transfer of dominion without splitting God in two.

isaiah-24-21-23.title: Isaiah 24:21-23
isaiah-24-21-23.summary: Yahweh punishes the host of heaven above and the kings of earth below, then reigns before His elders.
isaiah-24-21-23.plain: The real question: why does this text judge sky-powers and earthly kings in the very same breath, as if they were the same kind of problem? A report saying “the executives and the faulty machines both failed inspection” only makes sense if the machines were also somebody's job to maintain. **Judging “the host of heaven” and “the kings of the earth” together only makes sense if both were handed responsibility, and both failed at it.** This card reads it as one failure at two levels, sky-powers and kings alike.
isaiah-24-21-23.prob: Heavenly powers and earthly kings are judged in one sentence, as though they were the same kind of problem.
isaiah-24-21-23.res: Delegated rule that went wrong at both levels makes the pairing ordinary rather than poetic.

deuteronomy-32-8-9.title: Deuteronomy 32:8-9
deuteronomy-32-8-9.summary: The Most High divided the nations, and the number He divided them by is where the whole argument turns.
deuteronomy-32-8-9.plain: The real question: did God divide the nations by Israel's future headcount, or hand them over to a council of spiritual beings? **Two handwritten copies of the same letter from your grandmother, one older and torn, one newer and complete, and they do not say the same thing in one line.** Nobody forged anything. Somebody copied something. Which one do you read at the funeral, and how do you decide? This card leans on the older, shorter copies: divine beings, not a future headcount.
deuteronomy-32-8-9.prob: The nations are divided according to a number, and on the traditional reading that number is Israel, who does not exist yet. The verse is dating the division of humanity to a yardstick that will not be born for generations.
deuteronomy-32-8-9.res: Divine beings as the number fits the table of nations in Genesis 10, explains the contrast in verse 9 where Yahweh keeps Jacob for Himself, and supplies the background that Deuteronomy 4:19, Daniel 10 and Acts 17 all assume.

deuteronomy-32-43-hebrews-1-6.title: Deuteronomy 32:43; Hebrews 1:6
deuteronomy-32-43-hebrews-1-6.summary: The end of the Song of Moses, where the Masoretic text is one line and every other witness is longer.
deuteronomy-32-43-hebrews-1-6.plain: The real question: did later copies of this song lose a line about angels worshiping God, or did earlier copies add one that was never there? **Imagine a will with six copies at six law offices. Five include a paragraph. The sixth (the one that became everyone's default) is missing it.** That's not proof the paragraph was added later; it could just as easily be the copy that lost something. This card takes the longer reading as original, and the shorter one as the copy that lost a line.
deuteronomy-32-43-hebrews-1-6.prob: Hebrews 1:6 quotes a line about all God's angels worshipping the Son and presents it as Scripture. That line is not in the Hebrew text behind the King James or most English Old Testaments.
deuteronomy-32-43-hebrews-1-6.res: If the longer text is original, Hebrews is quoting Deuteronomy as it stood in the first century, and the chapter lost divine beings at two points rather than one. That also explains why the Song of Moses ends on a cosmic note instead of a national one, which fits how it opened.

deuteronomy-4-19-20.title: Deuteronomy 4:19-20
deuteronomy-4-19-20.summary: Israel must not worship the host of heaven, which Yahweh allotted to all the other peoples.
deuteronomy-4-19-20.plain: The real question: if God really handed the sky-powers to the other nations, why is it wrong for Israel to worship them too? A parent gives each kid their own chore and their own allowance: one kid can't then claim a sibling's allowance too, even though the money is just as real either way. **What was handed to someone else stays off limits to you, precisely because it was never yours to begin with.** This card reads the sky-powers as real, delegated rulers over the nations, not just stars.
deuteronomy-4-19-20.prob: God is said to have assigned the host of heaven to the nations, and then forbids Israel the same thing. An assignment is not a prohibition, so what was given to them.
deuteronomy-4-19-20.res: Delegated authority over the nations makes the sentence read straight. What Israel may not do is worship what the others were placed under.

genesis-11-1-9.title: Genesis 11:1-9
genesis-11-1-9.summary: Babel, the scattering, and the moment the nations are set aside.
genesis-11-1-9.plain: The real question: why does one tower-building project end with the founding of every nation on earth? Isn't that wildly out of proportion? **Grounding one kid for breaking curfew and then reorganizing the entire household's chore chart is a strange response, unless the reorganizing was the actual point and the grounding was only the occasion for it.** This story reads the same way once you notice how much bigger the outcome is than the offense. This card reads Babel as the moment the nations were handed off, not a fable about language.
genesis-11-1-9.prob: The punishment for building a tower is the creation of the nations, which reads as disproportionate unless something else is happening.
genesis-11-1-9.res: Read as the disinheritance behind Deuteronomy 32, Babel produces the map that the rest of the Old Testament assumes, and Pentecost becomes its answer rather than a coincidence.

daniel-10-13-20-21.title: Daniel 10:13, 20-21
daniel-10-13-20-21.summary: A prince of Persia resists for twenty-one days, a prince of Greece is coming, and Michael fights for Israel.
daniel-10-13-20-21.plain: The real question: what could possibly hold up a heavenly messenger for three weeks, if the only players are God and humans? A diplomat can be delayed for weeks by a hostile foreign office: not because the office is physically stronger, but because it has real jurisdiction there. **A messenger stopped for twenty-one days by something called “the prince of Persia” reads like exactly that kind of territorial standoff, not an empty hallway with nothing in it.** This card reads the “princes” as real territorial powers, not human kings.
daniel-10-13-20-21.prob: A messenger from God is delayed three weeks by something called the prince of Persia, and needs help to get through. Nothing in a flat angelology explains a delay.
daniel-10-13-20-21.res: Territorial powers with actual jurisdiction account for the delay, the naming by nation, and Michael's specific attachment to Israel.

acts-17-26-27.title: Acts 17:26-27
acts-17-26-27.summary: Paul tells the Areopagus that God fixed the times and the boundaries of the nations.
acts-17-26-27.plain: The real question: is Paul just describing ordinary history, or is he announcing that an actual, standing arrangement over the nations is being cancelled? **Announcing “the old lease is up” only lands as news if there really was a lease.** Paul tells a pagan crowd that God fixed the nations' boundaries, then pivots straight into an announcement. That only makes sense as news if the boundaries were the real thing, not just a figure of speech. This card reads Paul as announcing the end of that arrangement, not narrating history.
acts-17-26-27.prob: Paul chooses allotment language in front of a pagan audience and then announces that the arrangement is ending.
acts-17-26-27.res: If the boundaries were an actual assignment, the sermon is an announcement that the assignment is being revoked, which is why he goes straight to the resurrection.

genesis-3-1-15.title: Genesis 3:1-15
genesis-3-1-15.summary: The nachash in the garden, and the sentence passed on it.
genesis-3-1-15.plain: The real question: is the speaking creature in the garden just an animal, or something else operating there with real authority? **A courtroom doesn't sentence a stray dog the way it sentences a person: the severity of a sentence tells you what kind of defendant is standing there.** The sentence this creature receives reads like it was written for someone who knew exactly what they were doing, not an animal that wandered in. This card reads the serpent as a real, rebellious spiritual being, not a literal snake.
genesis-3-1-15.prob: A creature inside sacred space speaks, knows what God said, and is sentenced in language that outruns anything you could say to an animal.
genesis-3-1-15.res: A divine rebel operating in Eden accounts for the access, the knowledge, the authority in the conversation, and the scope of the curse.

ezekiel-28-11-19.title: Ezekiel 28:11-19
ezekiel-28-11-19.summary: A guardian cherub in Eden, on the holy mountain, cast out for pride.
ezekiel-28-11-19.plain: The real question: is this really about Satan's fall from heaven, or a human king mocked with borrowed, older imagery? **A political cartoon draws a stubborn official as a mule, ears and all.** Nobody thinks he actually has hooves. The artist borrowed a shape everyone already recognizes to land one point. A writer aimed a poem at a real king the same way, dressing him in older, half-remembered imagery about a magnificent guardian's fall. The costume is the insult. This card reads the passage as borrowed cosmic imagery aimed at a human king, not Satan's biography.
ezekiel-28-11-19.prob: The oracle is addressed to the king of Tyre and then describes him in Eden, on the mountain of God, as an anointed cherub. The description overshoots the addressee.
ezekiel-28-11-19.res: A known cosmic rebel story used as the template for a taunt against a king explains both layers without making either one disappear.

isaiah-14-12-15.title: Isaiah 14:12-15
isaiah-14-12-15.summary: Helel ben-shachar, shining one, son of the dawn, falls from heaven.
isaiah-14-12-15.plain: The real question: is “Lucifer” a name for Satan, or a title mocking a human king with borrowed legend? Call someone **"the guy who flew too close to the sun"** and everyone hears the insult, no myth lecture needed: the doomed-flight story does the work by itself. An old poem mocks a real king the same way, dressing him as a legendary figure who tried to rule the sky and fell. The costume carries the insult, not a biography. Same move as the Ezekiel taunt: a human king in borrowed legend, not Satan's origin story.
isaiah-14-12-15.prob: A taunt song against the king of Babylon suddenly describes someone trying to set a throne above the stars of God, then verse 16 has onlookers staring at a man.
isaiah-14-12-15.res: A cosmic rebel motif borrowed to mock a human king holds both halves at once, which is exactly what the genre of a mashal does.

genesis-6-1-4.title: Genesis 6:1-4
genesis-6-1-4.summary: The sons of God take wives, and the Nephilim are in the earth.
genesis-6-1-4.plain: The real question: were the “sons of God” who married human women fallen spiritual beings, or just powerful human rulers? Someone tells the neighbourhood story about the founding family, all heroism and destiny. **You tell the same events back with the same names and every detail intact, and in your version they come off badly.** You have not invented anything. You have retold their story against them. This card reads the “sons of God” as real spiritual beings, retelling an old story as an indictment.
genesis-6-1-4.prob: Four verses interrupt a genealogy, introduce a category of being, produce offspring the text calls mighty men of renown, and then the flood arrives. The passage is doing work in the narrative and a flat reading leaves it doing none.
genesis-6-1-4.res: The supernatural reading is the one that pays across the whole canon rather than in one place. It explains the interruption, the Nephilim, the giant clans in Numbers and Joshua, the conquest rationale, Jude and 2 Peter, the demonology the Gospels assume, and the unanimous Second Temple understanding. No other reading reaches more than two of those.

jude-6-2-peter-2-4.title: Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4
jude-6-2-peter-2-4.summary: Angels who abandoned their proper dwelling, held in chains until judgment.
jude-6-2-peter-2-4.plain: The real question: what specific, well-known story are these two writers assuming their readers already know, without ever spelling it out? **Someone at a family gathering says, “well, you remember what happened at Thanksgiving,” and everyone nods. The story never gets retold because the whole room already owns it.** These two writers mention an angelic rebellion the same way: assumed, not narrated. This card reads that assumed story as Genesis 6, read the way the first century read it.
jude-6-2-peter-2-4.prob: Two writers refer to an angelic sin as something their readers already know, and never explain it. The reference assumes a story.
jude-6-2-peter-2-4.res: Genesis 6 as read in the Second Temple period supplies the story both writers assume, which is why neither felt the need to narrate it.

jude-14-15.title: Jude 14-15
jude-14-15.summary: Jude quotes Enoch, the seventh from Adam, by name.
jude-14-15.plain: The real question: does quoting a book by name as prophecy mean the writer considered that whole book equally authoritative? A speaker can quote one line from a well-known poem, name the poet, and call the line true, without thereby declaring the poet's entire body of work equally authoritative. **Quoting one line and naming its source is not the same act as officially canonizing everything that source ever wrote.** This card reads the quotation as evidence of what the first century actually read, not an endorsement of a whole book.
jude-14-15.prob: A canonical letter quotes a non-canonical book as prophecy, by name, without apology.
jude-14-15.res: Taking it as evidence of what the first century read, rather than as a problem to be managed, explains the quotation and the surrounding argument at once.

numbers-13-33.title: Numbers 13:33
numbers-13-33.summary: The spies report the Nephilim, the sons of Anak, and call themselves grasshoppers.
numbers-13-33.plain: The real question: were there really still giant clans in the land, or are these just scared scouts exaggerating? **A news story can quote an eyewitness by name and still say, a paragraph later, that the account was exaggerated.** Quoting someone isn't the same as endorsing them: the story reports the claim, it doesn't confirm it. An old account does exactly this: it records what a group of scouts said, then flatly calls their report a bad one. This card still takes the giant clans as continuous with Genesis 6, even inside an unreliable report.
numbers-13-33.prob: A word from before the flood turns up in a reconnaissance report centuries after it, in a land Israel is about to enter.
numbers-13-33.res: Continuity between Genesis 6 and the giant clans gives the conquest a rationale that is theological rather than ethnic, and explains why particular regions get particular language.

joshua-11-21-22.title: Joshua 11:21-22
joshua-11-21-22.summary: Joshua cuts off the Anakim from the hill country, and none are left except in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod.
joshua-11-21-22.plain: The real question: why does one specific group get its own separate wrap-up, naming exactly where its survivors ended up? A report on a completed evacuation that adds “except for a few families who relocated to three named towns” is setting something up for later: that kind of specificity is a promise, not filler. **Naming exactly where the last of the Anakim went reads the same way: a loose thread, left for later.** This card reads that loose thread as pointing straight at Goliath.
joshua-11-21-22.prob: The narrator gives the Anakim their own summary statement, separate from the general conquest account, and then names exactly where survivors remain.
joshua-11-21-22.res: A targeted objective explains the separate summary and sets up Goliath of Gath without anyone having to reach for it later.

leviticus-16-8-10.title: Leviticus 16:8-10
leviticus-16-8-10.summary: One goat for Yahweh, one goat for Azazel, sent into the wilderness.
leviticus-16-8-10.plain: The real question: is Azazel a place the goat gets sent to, or a being the goat gets sent away from? **One ticket for Dave, the other ticket for the bin.** That sentence is lopsided and your ear catches it. **One ticket for Dave, the other for Susan** is not. When a sentence sets up two slots the same way, both slots normally hold the same kind of thing. This card reads Azazel as a being, not a place, to keep that parallel intact.
leviticus-16-8-10.prob: The verse builds a parallel, one lot for the LORD and one lot for Azazel. If Azazel is a place, the parallel is between a person and a location, which is not how the sentence is built.
leviticus-16-8-10.res: Azazel as a named being keeps the grammatical parallel intact and connects the wilderness destination to the place where the Second Temple material says the rebel was bound.

mark-5-1-20.title: Mark 5:1-20
mark-5-1-20.summary: Legion, in Gentile territory east of the lake, begging not to be sent to the abyss.
mark-5-1-20.plain: The real question: why do the demons in this story beg for a temporary home in pigs instead of the place they clearly already know about and dread? **Someone begging for a bunk instead of being sent back to one specific address only makes sense if that address is real, and they know exactly what's waiting there.** These spirits negotiate like prisoners avoiding a real transfer, not vague evil in the abstract. This card reads that address as the same confinement described in the Second Temple Watchers material.
mark-5-1-20.prob: The demons want a body badly enough to ask for pigs, and they know there is a specific place they can be sent instead.
mark-5-1-20.res: A demonology in which these spirits are disembodied and awaiting confinement explains both the request and the dread, and explains why the scene is staged outside Israel.

1-samuel-28-13.title: 1 Samuel 28:13
1-samuel-28-13.summary: The medium at Endor sees an elohim coming up out of the earth, and it is Samuel.
1-samuel-28-13.plain: The real question: did the medium actually see a god, or does the word just mean “someone from the realm of the dead”? **Category words don't rank things: "vehicle" covers a skateboard and a jet, with no claim about which matters more.** Imagine your only word for a dead person worked as a category too, usable the instant someone was gone, without claiming anything about their importance. An old story uses that kind of word for someone who just died, naming the category, not the rank. This card reads “a god” the same way: a real category word, not a claim about status.
1-samuel-28-13.prob: A dead prophet is called elohim. If the word means deity by rank, the sentence is impossible.
1-samuel-28-13.res: Elohim as a term marking which realm a being inhabits rather than its rank lets this verse, Psalm 82 and Deuteronomy 32 all use the word consistently.

john-10-31-36.title: John 10:31-36
john-10-31-36.summary: Jesus answers a charge of blasphemy by quoting Psalm 82.
john-10-31-36.plain: The real question: why does quoting one old psalm about “gods” work as a legal defense against a charge of blasphemy? **Quoting one line from an old court ruling only defuses an accusation if the judge already knows that ruling and accepts it as binding.** Say it to someone unfamiliar with the case and it lands as nothing. A speaker facing a serious accusation here reaches for one old, short line, and it works: that only makes sense if the room already recognized it as authoritative. This card reads that recognition as proof a real divine-council reading was common ground at the time.
john-10-31-36.prob: Under a charge that carries the death penalty, Jesus reaches for an obscure psalm about gods. The defense only works if his accusers already understood it.
john-10-31-36.res: A live divine council framework in the first century explains why the quotation functions as a defense at all.

matthew-1-1-6.title: Matthew 1:1-6
matthew-1-1-6.summary: Four women named in the genealogy of Jesus, each with an irregular story.
matthew-1-1-6.plain: The real question: why does a genealogy that normally lists only men suddenly name four women, each with an irregular story attached? **A family tree that skips every in-law except four, and all four carry some kind of scandal, is not an accident: someone chose to include them, and chose them as a matched set.** The question is what that set is pointing back to. This card reads it as a deliberate echo of the Genesis 6 pattern.
matthew-1-1-6.prob: Genealogies of this kind do not usually name women. These four are named and the obvious candidates are not.
matthew-1-1-6.res: Heiser proposes the four would have called the Genesis 6 pattern to mind for a first century reader.

matthew-16-13-20.title: Matthew 16:13-20
matthew-16-13-20.summary: Caesarea Philippi, the gates of Hades, and the confession.
matthew-16-13-20.plain: The real question: why does the writer bother naming the exact location for this exchange, and what does that location have to do with talk of “gates”? **A story that specifies “he said it standing on the courthouse steps” wants you to notice the courthouse: the location is doing work the plain words alone don't do.** This spot is named on purpose, right before Jesus starts talking about gates that will not hold. This card reads the location as deliberate: a real site tied to the underworld in local belief.
matthew-16-13-20.prob: Matthew tells us where this happened, which he rarely bothers to do, and the saying that follows is about gates.
matthew-16-13-20.res: The location is doing work. Jesus asks at the foot of Hermon, in front of a cave locals treated as an entrance to the underworld, then names gates that will not hold.

matthew-17-1-8.title: Matthew 17:1-8
matthew-17-1-8.summary: The transfiguration, six days later, on a high mountain.
matthew-17-1-8.plain: The real question: does it matter which mountain this is, or is “a high mountain” just scenery? **A story that says “they drove to a house” right after three pages at one specific address is quietly still talking about that same house.** This mountain scene follows immediately after one tied to a very particular place, where location was already doing real work. This card reads the unnamed mountain as Hermon, reclaiming the site of the Watchers' oath.
matthew-17-1-8.prob: The mountain is unnamed, the timing is marked precisely, and the location follows immediately from Caesarea Philippi.
matthew-17-1-8.res: Hermon as the mountain turns the scene into a reclaiming of the place where the Watchers swore their oath, which is where Reversing Hermon gets its title.

luke-10-1-20.title: Luke 10:1-20
luke-10-1-20.summary: Seventy sent out, and Satan falling like lightning when they return.
luke-10-1-20.plain: The real question: why does a specific head-count and a comment about a cosmic fall show up back to back, as if they're one report and not two? **A manager sending exactly the right number of reps to cover every territory on the map, then getting a call that the old regional boss just got fired, is one story, not two unrelated updates.** The number and the falling-star line read like a single status report. This card reads the two halves as one announcement about the nations' allotment.
luke-10-1-20.prob: The number is specified and then Jesus responds to a report about demons with a statement about a fall from heaven. The two halves want a connection.
luke-10-1-20.res: A mission sized to the nations of Genesis 10 makes the number meaningful and makes the reply a status report on the allotment rather than a change of subject.

ephesians-6-10-12.title: Ephesians 6:10-12
ephesians-6-10-12.summary: The struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers, authorities, and cosmic powers.
ephesians-6-10-12.plain: The real question: what is this list of “rulers, authorities, cosmic powers” actually naming, and why does the writer never stop to explain any of it? **A memo that says “route this past Legal, Compliance, and the Regional Director” assumes you already know the org chart: the writer isn't inventing categories, just naming positions everyone in the building already recognizes.** This list works the same way: ordinary vocabulary to the writer, foreign to us. This card reads it as a real chain of command that rebelled, not rhetorical flourish.
ephesians-6-10-12.prob: Paul names four categories of hostile authority and places them in the heavenly realms, as though the reader already knows the org chart.
ephesians-6-10-12.res: A structure of delegated rule that rebelled makes the categories ordinary vocabulary rather than rhetorical flourish, and explains why Paul can list them without defining them.

1-corinthians-11-10.title: 1 Corinthians 11:10
1-corinthians-11-10.summary: A woman ought to have authority on her head, because of the angels.
1-corinthians-11-10.plain: The real question: what do angels have to do with head coverings? What is Paul assuming his readers already know? **"Obviously, because of the Petersons, knock before entering."** If you weren't there for that incident, the reason makes no sense: the writer assumes a shared story never retold. One line in an old letter works the same way: the reason survives, the background everyone in the room already knew does not. This card reads the missing background as the Watchers story Paul's readers already knew.
1-corinthians-11-10.prob: The clause because of the angels has no antecedent anywhere in the letter and no obvious relevance to head covering.
1-corinthians-11-10.res: If Paul assumes the Watchers story, the clause has a referent and the instruction has a reason.

1-peter-3-18-22.title: 1 Peter 3:18-22
1-peter-3-18-22.summary: Christ proclaims to the spirits in prison, the ones disobedient in the days of Noah.
1-peter-3-18-22.plain: The real question: why does the writer date this group's disobedience to one specific, ancient moment, instead of just saying “sinful people” in general? **Dating a group to one exact, ancient event, instead of describing them in general terms, is how you'd refer to a specific incident everyone already had a name for, not a vague category.** These “spirits in prison” are pinned to the days of Noah with exactly that kind of precision. This card reads them as those same imprisoned rebels from Genesis 6.
1-peter-3-18-22.prob: Peter dates the disobedience of the spirits to the days of Noah, which is a strange way to identify human souls and a precise way to identify something else.
1-peter-3-18-22.res: Imprisoned rebels from Genesis 6 explain the dating, the prison, and why a proclamation rather than an offer.
